content: The provided text appears to be a mix of bibliographic references, search strategies, and systematic review methodologies related to indoor heat, housing, and health. 1. Von Seidlein (2013) explored strategies to design low-cost housing in tropical climates that are not only healthy but also comfortable. This study was published in Tropical Medicine and International Health. 2. Von Wichert (2008) examined the significance of atmospheric heat waves on health services, particularly in populations already affected by altered health conditions. This research was detailed in Medizinische Klinik. 3. Mason and Macfarlane (2011) conducted a literature review on health promotion interventions addressing climate change through a primary healthcare approach. Their findings were published in the Health Promotion Journal of Australia. 4. Macfarlane (2013) investigated the transformation of raw smart home data into health metrics, with a focus on the Great Northern Haven project. This work was presented in the Irish Journal of Medical Science. 5. White-Newsome and Sanchez (2012) analyzed the impact of indoor heat exposure on vulnerable populations in the context of climate change. Their study appeared in Environmental Research. 6. A 2011 study assessed heat-adaptive behaviors among older adults living in urban environments, with findings published in Maturitas. 7. Hansen (2013) provided insights into the perspectives of health service providers in rural and remote South Australian communities regarding extreme heat and its health implications. This research was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 8. Jacobs et al. (2014) investigated whether residential energy conservation measures improve health outcomes. Their study, titled Watts-to-Wellbeing, was published in Energy Efficiency. 9. Yudhastuti (2008) examined the relationship between housing sanitation and acute respiratory tract infections among undergraduate students in Indonesia. This study was published in the Asia-Pacific Journal of Public Health. 10. Horton, Coull, and Gold (2014) conducted a repeated-measures study on the effects of ambient pollution, temperature, and humidity on brachial artery responses in individuals with type 2 diabetes. Their findings were published in Environmental Health Perspectives. 11. Gronlund (2013) explored how personal and small-area characteristics modify susceptibility to mortality during extreme weather events. This research was published in Epidemiology. 12. Zuluaga and Rodriguez-Artalejo (2011) investigated the association between housing conditions and mortality in older patients hospitalized for heart failure. Their findings were published in the American Heart Journal. 13. A systematic review was conducted to inform the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines, focusing on the impact of indoor heat on health outcomes. This review included a comprehensive search strategy and was updated in April 2018. 14. The search strategy for the systematic review included terms related to housing (e.g., house, housing, home, residence, building, shelter) and environmental factors (e.g., ventilation, air conditioning, humidity, heating, temperature). The search was conducted across multiple databases, including PAIS Index and Web of Science, with a focus on publications from 2015 to 2018. 15. The review also considered studies on indoor temperature, heat exposure, heat waves, thermal stress, and air conditioning, aiming to identify relevant evidence for the WHO guidelines. 16. Duplicate records were removed during the search process, and the final results were screened for relevance to the topic of indoor heat and health.
